hello.note: For anyone, at any time of day. Iranians greet warmly and often add خوش آمدید (KHOSH aa-ma-DEED), welcome

how-are-you.note: Polite, with شما (sho-MAA), the respectful you. Friends say خوبی؟ (KHOO-bee), are you good?

im-well.note: The same for a man or a woman: Persian has no he or she, and no men's and women's forms

good-night.note: Good evening and good night, both meeting and parting

thank-you.note: Merci (MER-see) is just as common. خیلی ممنون (KHEY-lee mam-NOON) means thank you very much

no.note: Careful: na sounds like yes in some languages. نه، ممنون (na, mam-NOON) is no, thank you

excuse-me.note: Sorry, and excuse me to get attention or get past

my-name.note: The name goes in the middle: the verb comes last in Persian. The audio uses Peter as the example name

where-from.note: Answer اهل ... هستم (AHL-e ... has-TAM), I'm from...

dont-understand.note: Literally "I don't follow", the same for a man or a woman

repeat.note: می‌شه...؟ (MEE-she), is it possible...?, starts a polite request

speak-english.note: Literally "do you know English?" Young people in cities often speak some

one.note: Persian digits are used on prices and signs: ۱ ۲ ۳ ۴ ۵ ۶ ۷ ۸ ۹ ۰

nine.note: Written like no, نه (na), but said differently

thousand.note: Prices are officially in rials, but people count in tomans, 10 rials each, and often drop the thousands: ask تومان یا ریال؟ (too-MAAN yaa ree-YAAL), tomans or rials?

how-much.note: Literally "what's its price?" Point at the thing

would-like.note: Literally "I wanted...", the polite way to order, the same for a man or a woman. The thing comes first; the audio uses یک چای (yek chaai), a tea

i-want.note: More direct. The audio uses این رو (EEN-ro), this one

do-you-have.note: The thing comes first. The audio uses آب (aab), water, as the example

discount.note: Bargaining is normal in the bazaar. If a seller says قابل نداره (GHAA-bel na-DAA-re), it's nothing, take it, that is taarof, ritual politeness: thank them and insist on paying

card.note: Foreign cards don't work in Iran. Bring cash (euros or dollars) to exchange, or buy a local tourist card

checkout-time.note: Literally "what time is handing back the room?"

breakfast.note: Iranian breakfast: flatbread, white cheese, walnuts, herbs and sweet tea

toilet.note: کجاست (ko-JAAST) means where is. Many toilets are squat toilets

taxi.note: Snapp, an Iranian ride app, is widely used. Agree the fare first in a street taxi

bus.note: Long-distance VIP buses are comfortable and cheap

bus-station.note: The long-distance bus terminal. Tehran has several, by direction

which-train.note: Literally "which is the ... train?" The audio uses اصفهان (es-fa-HAAN), Isfahan, as the example

two-tickets.note: The audio uses Isfahan as the example
two-tickets.spoken: دو تا بلیط برای اصفهان، لطفاً

trip-length.note: The audio uses Isfahan as the example

allergic.note: The food goes in the middle, the same for a man or a woman. Add: ماهی (maa-HEE) fish, آجیل (aa-JEEL) nuts, بادام‌زمینی (baa-daam-za-mee-NEE) peanuts. The audio uses peanuts

love-dish.note: Literally "I fell in love with this food", a warm compliment

what-called.note: Point at the dish or item

table-for-two.text: یک میز برای دو نفر، لطفاً
table-for-two.say: yek MEEZ ba-RAA-ye DO na-FAR, LOT-fan
table-for-two.note: For more people: سه نفر (SE na-FAR), 3, or چهار نفر (cha-HAAR na-FAR), 4

beer.note: Alcohol is illegal in Iran. Maa-osh-sha-eer is non-alcoholic malt beer, sold everywhere in many flavours

coffee.note: Tea is far more common, but cafés with good coffee are everywhere in the cities

tea.note: Served all day, strong and without milk, often with a sugar cube, قند (ghand), held between the teeth

milk.note: Also means lion, and tap: the same word

hot.note: Hot to touch. Hot weather is گرم (garm). Spicy is تند (tond)

cheers.note: Said to someone eating: enjoy it. To raise a glass of tea or juice, سلامتی (sa-laa-ma-TEE), to health

help.note: Shout it. The police are on 110

need-doctor.note: The same for a man or a woman. For an ambulance, call 115

pharmacy.note: Many pharmacies are open late, and some 24 hours (شبانه‌روزی, sha-baa-ne-roo-ZEE)
